summary: Gives an overview and explanatory background for the revised IDNA system, covering issues that emerged after the original internationalized domain name protocol was deployed, including keeping up with newer Unicode versions. It is informational and explains the rationale behind the revision.

plainLanguage.summary: IDNA lets applications use many non-ASCII characters in domain names while keeping DNS labels in an ASCII-compatible form. This RFC explains why the rules were revised and what trade-offs the new design makes.

questions: what is the difference between idna2003 and idna2008
why are symbols not allowed in domain names
subtitle: Why the rules for internationalized domain names were revised

tldr.problem: IDNA2003 depended on Unicode 3.2 and mapped user input in ways that could lose distinctions between characters. The protocol needed to accommodate newer Unicode characters and clarify character validity.
tldr.mechanism: IDNA2008 uses Unicode-property rules to include valid characters, separates registration from lookup, and leaves user-input mapping to applications rather than requiring protocol mapping.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC explains the design rationale. The normative IDNA2008 rules are in the other documents in the series, not here.

today: RFC 5894 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text says that normative IDNA2008 conformance rules are in the other documents in the series.

sections.title: What IDNA Does
sections.content:
Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA) lets a client application convert a Unicode domain label into an ASCII-compatible form called an A-label. A-labels begin with xn-- and use Punycode. Because DNS receives the ASCII form, IDNA does not require changes to DNS servers or the DNS protocol.

IDNA2003 was defined in a set of documents and depended on Unicode 3.2. IDNA2008 keeps the Punycode encoding but changes the rules for character validity and mapping. This RFC provides background and rationale only; conformance rules are specified in the other IDNA2008 documents.
sections.plainLanguage: IDNA lets a website name contain characters beyond ASCII by converting each label to an ASCII-compatible form for DNS. This RFC explains the revised rules but is not itself a specification to implement.

sections.title: How IDNA2008 Classifies Characters
sections.content:
IDNA2008 uses an inclusion model: a Unicode code point is invalid unless a property-based rule or an explicit exception includes it. It groups code points as PROTOCOL-VALID, CONTEXTUAL RULE REQUIRED, DISALLOWED or UNASSIGNED. A protocol-valid character may still be limited by context or whole-label rules, and a registry may apply stricter registration policy.

Contextual characters need a rule to establish whether they are valid in a label. The RFC discusses zero-width joiner and non-joiner as examples. Disallowed characters include many compatibility forms, case-folded forms, symbols and punctuation. Unassigned code points are excluded until Unicode assigns them and the tables classify them.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules put each character into a category. Some characters are allowed, some need a specific context, and others are excluded until a Unicode version assigns and classifies them.

sections.title: Registration, Lookup and User Input
sections.content:
IDNA2008 separates registration from lookup because registries apply local policy when names are registered, while clients look up labels. Registries are expected to accept exact valid A-labels and may restrict which otherwise-valid labels they register. Lookup applications use a narrower set of protocol checks and should not apply every registry-specific rule.

IDNA2008 does not prescribe character mappings. An application or its input method may map user input before calling IDNA, for example to account for local keyboard or language conventions. Applications may display A-labels or Unicode U-labels, but the RFC says A-labels are opaque and normally should not be the default display.
sections.plainLanguage: Registries decide which valid names they will sell, while lookup software checks whether a name can be processed by the protocol. An application may adjust what a person types before applying IDNA rules.

sections.title: Compatibility with IDNA2003
sections.content:
IDNA2003 mapped Eszett to ss, Greek Final Sigma to medial Sigma, and zero-width joiner and non-joiner to nothing. IDNA2008 treats Eszett and Final Sigma as distinct protocol-valid characters and gives the joiner characters contextual treatment. As a result, some labels may have different interpretations or A-labels across the two versions.

The working group decided that these changes did not justify changing the xn-- prefix. A prefix change would require systems to try multiple encodings, complicate DNS caching and create opportunities for confusion. The RFC describes registry transition choices, including restricting new characters, giving existing registrants priority, using variants or ignoring the conflict.
sections.plainLanguage: A few characters no longer map to other characters as they did in IDNA2003. Registries must consider how to handle names that could conflict, but the overall A-label prefix stays the same.

sections.title: Character Policy and Security Context
sections.content:
The RFC explains why symbols are excluded: several different code points can look or sound like the same symbol, making names difficult to identify and communicate reliably. Registries are expected to choose policies that reduce confusion, including considering mixed scripts and characters familiar to the registry's language context.

Existing DNS servers receive A-labels rather than Unicode forms. The security section says this document is explanatory and introduces no new security issues; implementing from it instead of the normative documents could cause interoperability or security problems. It also describes character and contextual-rule registries maintained for IDNA.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules exclude some characters because people may not be able to distinguish or communicate them reliably. This RFC explains the reasoning; implementers need the normative IDNA documents for exact behavior.

viz.caption: The four character categories described for IDNA2008

items.label: Protocol-valid
items.desc: Allowed subject to any applicable label or context rules.

items.label: Context rule required
items.desc: Allowed only when an associated rule permits the character.

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: Not yet assigned in the Unicode version being used.
